title: How to Clean a Cast Iron Skillet Without Ruining the Seasoning
hook: A cast iron skillet can outlive you. Most people ruin theirs in the sink in under a year. In the next few minutes you'll learn the seven steps that keep a skillet black, slick and rust free for decades.
intro: Cast iron is not like a regular non-stick pan. The non-stick surface is a thin layer of baked-on oil called the seasoning, and every wash either builds it up or strips it away. The good news is that cleaning it properly takes about five minutes and needs almost nothing you don't already have in your kitchen.
youNeed: A stiff brush or pan scraper
youNeedNarration: Here's everything you'll need. Coarse salt, which works as a gentle abrasive. A little neutral oil, like canola, vegetable or flaxseed. A clean, lint-free towel. And a stiff brush or a plastic pan scraper for anything stubborn. That's it.
heroImageQuery: cast iron skillet on wooden table
heroImagePrompt: A well seasoned black cast iron skillet resting on a rustic wooden kitchen counter, soft morning side light, shallow depth of field, warm cream tones, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Rinse it while it's still warm
steps.narration: Step one. Clean the skillet while it is still warm, right after cooking. Run hot water over it and use your brush or scraper to lift the loose food. Warm iron releases residue far more easily than cold iron, and a quick rinse now saves you a scrubbing session later. If the pan is screaming hot, let it cool for a couple of minutes first, because a blast of cold water on very hot iron can crack it.
steps.tip: Warm pan, hot water, no shock
steps.mistake: Pouring cold water on a smoking hot pan
steps.imageQuery: rinsing cast iron skillet hot water sink
steps.imagePrompt: Hands rinsing a black cast iron skillet under running hot water in a farmhouse sink, steam rising, warm kitchen light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Scrub with coarse salt
steps.narration: Step two. For anything that didn't rinse off, pour in a generous handful of coarse salt and a splash of water. Work it around with a towel or your brush in small circles. The salt grains scrub away stuck-on bits without cutting into the seasoning the way a steel scouring pad would. When the salt turns brown, you've picked up the grime. Rinse it out and check the surface.
steps.mistake: Using a steel wool pad on the cooking surface
steps.imageQuery: coarse salt cast iron pan scrubbing
steps.imagePrompt: Close-up of coarse sea salt being rubbed in a black cast iron skillet with a folded kitchen towel, overhead view, warm tones, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Boil off stubborn residue
steps.narration: Step three. Stuck-on food that won't budge gets the boiling trick. Add a centimetre of water to the pan, put it back on the stove and bring it to a simmer for two or three minutes. The heat and the water loosen the burnt layer, and a gentle nudge with a wooden spatula lifts it right off. Pour the water out and move on. Never let the pan sit in that water once the heat is off.
steps.tip: Two minutes of simmering beats ten of scrubbing
steps.mistake: Letting the pan soak after boiling
steps.imageQuery: cast iron skillet boiling water stove
steps.imagePrompt: A cast iron skillet on a gas stove with a shallow layer of water gently simmering, small bubbles, blue flame visible, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Dry it completely on the stove
steps.narration: Step four. Towel-dry the skillet, then put it back on a medium burner for one or two minutes. You want every trace of moisture gone, including the water hiding in the pores of the iron that a towel can't reach. When the surface looks dull and dry all the way across, and the handle is warm to the touch, you're ready for oil. Moisture is the single biggest cause of rust, so don't skip this.
steps.imageQuery: cast iron skillet drying stove heat
steps.imagePrompt: A dry black cast iron skillet sitting on a lit stove burner, slight heat shimmer, dark kitchen background, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Wipe on a thin coat of oil
steps.narration: Step five. While the pan is still warm, pour in about a teaspoon of neutral oil. Use a folded paper towel to spread it over the entire cooking surface, up the sides and across the handle. Then take a fresh towel and wipe it all back off, as if you had made a mistake. The microscopic layer left behind is exactly the right amount. If the pan looks shiny or wet, there's too much oil.
steps.tip: Wipe it on, then wipe it off
steps.mistake: Leaving a thick, sticky layer of oil
steps.imageQuery: oiling cast iron skillet paper towel
steps.imagePrompt: A hand with a folded paper towel wiping a thin sheen of oil onto a black cast iron skillet, glossy surface, warm light, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Heat until it just starts to smoke
steps.narration: Step six. Put the oiled skillet back on the burner and turn the heat up. In a minute or two you'll see a faint wisp of smoke. That means the oil has reached its smoke point and is bonding to the iron, which is what actually builds the seasoning. Let it go for about thirty seconds, then turn off the heat. Doing this after every wash is how a pan gets that deep, glassy black finish.
steps.tip: A wisp of smoke means it's working
steps.mistake: Turning off the heat before the oil smokes
steps.imageQuery: cast iron skillet smoking seasoning stove
steps.imagePrompt: A cast iron skillet on a stove with a faint wisp of smoke rising, dark moody kitchen, light from the window, photorealistic, no text

steps.title: Store it dry and uncovered
steps.narration: Step seven. Let the skillet cool completely, then store it somewhere dry. Leave the lid off so air can circulate, and if you stack other pans inside it, slide a paper towel in between to protect the surface. Avoid cupboards right under the sink or next to the dishwasher, where humidity collects. A pan stored this way will be ready to cook the moment you take it out.
steps.mistake: Storing it with the lid on while still warm
steps.imageQuery: cast iron skillet hanging kitchen wall
steps.imagePrompt: Several black cast iron skillets hanging on hooks on a cream kitchen wall, tidy and dry, soft daylight, photorealistic, no text

mistakesToAvoid.narration: Now, the three mistakes that ruin more skillets than anything else. One, soaking. Even an hour in the sink starts rust. Two, the dishwasher. The detergent and the long steam cycle strip the seasoning completely. And three, putting it away wet. If you remember nothing else, remember this: cast iron never sits in water, and it never goes to bed damp.
items: Soaking the pan in the sink
Putting it away even slightly damp

recap.narration: Let's run through the whole routine one more time. Rinse it warm. Scrub with coarse salt. Boil off anything stubborn. Dry it on the stove. Wipe on a thin coat of oil. Heat it until it just smokes. And store it dry and uncovered. Seven steps, five minutes, and a skillet that gets better every single year.

outro: That's how you clean a cast iron skillet without ruining the seasoning. If this saved your pan, subscribe to WikiTube, we publish a new how-to every single day. And tell us in the comments what you want us to explain next. See you tomorrow.

metadata.title: How to Clean a Cast Iron Skillet Without Ruining the Seasoning (7 Steps)
metadata.description:
Cast iron lasts a lifetime, if you clean it right. In this video you'll learn the 7 steps to clean a cast iron skillet after cooking, dry it properly, re-season it in two minutes and store it so it never rusts. No soap debates, no steel wool, no dishwasher.

You'll need: coarse salt, a little neutral oil, a lint-free towel and a stiff brush or pan scraper.
